docs.title: Rust Programming: From Zero to Useful
docs.text: Learn Rust from first principles to a small command-line application.

docs.title: Course target
docs.text: By the end, you will be able to write, test, and package small Rust programs with confidence.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
This course is for programmers who are new to Rust. You should be comfortable with a terminal and basic programming ideas such as variables, functions, and conditionals. Install the stable Rust toolchain with rustup before starting.

Start with Module 0: First lesson, then use the roadmap and syllabus to plan the track.

docs.title: Final goal
docs.text:
Build a tested command-line task tracker while learning Rust's ownership model, types, error handling, and project tooling.

Milestone Modules Outcome Foundation 0–2 Compile Rust, use core types, and understand ownership. Application 3–4 Handle errors and organize code into a Cargo project. Capstone 5+ Build and test a useful command-line task tracker.

docs.title: Recommended sequence
docs.text:
1. Start with Module 0 and compile every example locally.
  2. Learn ownership before borrowing, collections, and error handling.
  3. Integrate each concept into the capstone only after the small example works.

docs.title: 0. Hello, Rust
docs.text:
• Install the toolchain and compile a first Rust program.
  • Read the shape of a main function and a println! macro.
  • Make a small change and observe the compiler feedback.

Add one section per module and link it to the module overview.

docs.title: Module 0: Set up Rust and build Hello World
By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Install the stable Rust toolchain with rustup.
  • Explain the jobs of rustup, rustc, and Cargo.
  • Build, run, format, check, and package a small application.

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Rust programs start at a function named main. The println! macro writes a line of text to the terminal. Rust checks the program before running it, so mistakes are reported early by the compiler.

flowchart LR
  A[main function] --> B[println! macro]
  B --> C[Compiled binary]

docs.title: Install the toolchain
docs.text:
The recommended installer is rustup. On Linux, macOS, or WSL, run:

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh

Accept the default stable toolchain, then open a new terminal so the Cargo bin directory is on your PATH. On Windows, download and run rustup-init.exe from the official installation page. Windows builds may also need the Visual Studio C++ build tools.

Verify the installation:

rustup show
rustc --version
cargo --version

Keep the stable toolchain current with rustup update. If a command is not found after installation, restart the terminal and check that $HOME/.cargo/bin is on PATH.

docs.title: The important commands
docs.text:
Command Job rustup Installs and selects Rust toolchains and components. rustc Compiles a Rust source file directly. cargo Creates, builds, runs, tests, documents, and packages projects. rustfmt Formats Rust source consistently. clippy Finds common mistakes and non-idiomatic Rust. rustdoc Generates API documentation from Rust comments. rust-analyzer Gives editor features such as completion and diagnostics.

The standard stable installation includes Cargo, rustfmt, and Clippy. If a component is missing, install it explicitly:

rustup component add rustfmt clippy
rustup component add rust-src  # useful for rust-analyzer

Most editors install or bundle rust-analyzer; VS Code uses the official extension. The compiler tools work independently of any editor.

docs.title: Create a Hello World application
docs.text:
Cargo keeps the source layout and build metadata together. From the repository root, create a new application in a temporary directory:

cargo new /tmp/hello-rust
cd /tmp/hello-rust

Cargo creates Cargo.toml and src/main.rs. Replace src/main.rs with:

fn main() {
    println!("Hello, Rust!");
}

docs.title: Build, run, and package it
docs.text:
Run these commands inside /tmp/hello-rust:

cargo check                 # type-check quickly without creating a binary
cargo build                 # debug build in target/debug/
cargo run                   # build if needed, then run the binary
cargo run -- Rust           # pass Rust as an argument to the binary
cargo build --release       # optimized build in target/release/
cargo test                  # run tests, when the project has tests
cargo doc --open            # build and open local API documentation
cargo package --allow-dirty # validate the package archive locally

For this application, the release binary is target/release/hello-rust on Linux and macOS, or target/release/hello-rust.exe on Windows. cargo package creates a crate archive for distribution and checks that the package can be published. It does not upload anything. Use cargo publish only when you intend to publish a crate to crates.io.

docs.title: Format and lint before sharing
docs.text:
cargo fmt                 # format the whole project
cargo fmt -- --check      # fail if formatting would change files
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings

rustfmt handles layout. Clippy provides advice about correctness, performance, and idiomatic style. Treat warnings as errors in CI when the project is ready for that policy.

The commands above are the standard Rust workflow: check, format, lint, test, build, then create a release artifact.

docs.title: Run the course example
docs.text:
The repository also contains a Cargo version of Hello World:

cargo run --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/hello-world/Cargo.toml

Expected output:

Hello, Rust!

docs.text: Change the message in examples/00-first-lesson/hello-world/src/main.rs, run cargo fmt, and use cargo run --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/hello-world/Cargo.toml to see the result.

docs.title: By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Explain ownership in one sentence.
  • Borrow a value with a reference.
  • Recognize why Rust prevents a dangling reference.

docs.title: The brief version
docs.text:
Ownership is Rust's rule for deciding which variable is responsible for a value. Every value has one owner. When the owner leaves its scope, Rust cleans up the value automatically.

Borrowing means using a reference to a value without taking ownership. &name creates a shared borrow, so a function can read a value while the caller keeps owning it. Rust checks that references never outlive the value they refer to.

flowchart LR
  O[Owner] -->|borrows with &| R[Reference]
  R -->|reads temporarily| V[Value]
  O -->|still owns| V

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
fn count_letters(text: &String) -> usize {
    text.len()
}

fn main() {
    let message = String::from("Rust");
    println!("{} has {} letters", message, count_letters(&message));
    println!("The owner can still use: {message}");
}

The function borrows message, so ownership stays in main. Compile and run the complete example from the repository root:

rustc examples/02-ownership-and-borrowing/main.rs -o /tmp/rust-ownership
/tmp/rust-ownership

Expected output:

Rust has 4 letters
The owner can still use: Rust

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Change count_letters to accept &str instead of &String. The call in main still works, and the function can now accept both string literals and String values.

docs.title: Checkpoint 1
docs.text:
Who is responsible for cleaning up a value?

Every reference The value's owner The compiler at random Check answer

docs.title: Checkpoint 2
docs.text:
What does `&message` create?

A shared borrow A second owner A copy of the string Check answer
